chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar from Muhammad ibn Isa from Amr ibn Sa'id who said: Ja'far ibn Ahmad wrote to him, asking him about travel and in what distance the shortening (of prayer) applies, so he wrote to him in his own hand, 'Peace be upon you,' and I recognize his handwriting, saying, 'The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him), when he traveled and went out on a journey, shortened (prayer) after one farsakh.' Then he repeated the question to him the following year, so he wrote to him, 'Peace be upon you,' 'In ten days.'

The meaning of these two reports in his saying (peace be upon him) 'he shortened after one farsakh,' and what followed their pattern among the reports, is that the distance, if it is at the limit at which shortening becomes obligatory or more, and the traveler travels for a day or more than that, then if he travels after that one farsakh or two farsakhs, shortening becomes obligatory upon him because the extent of the journey has reached a limit at which shortening is obligatory. And the consideration is not by what the person walks, but the consideration is by the intended distance, even if the person does not walk it in one go or one day. And this interpretation does not contradict what was narrated:

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: The Commander of the Faithful (Imam Ali)
key_terms.التَّقْصِيرُ: Shortening of the four-rak'ah prayers to two rak'ahs during travel
key_terms.الْمَسَافَةِ الْمَقْصُودَةِ: The intended distance of the journey

ai.seo_question: When does the obligation to shorten prayers begin during a journey?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the jurisprudential principle that the obligation of shortening prayers (qasr al-salat) is determined by the intended travel distance rather than the actual distance covered in a single day. It highlights the scholarly consensus that once the threshold for travel is met and the traveler has journeyed for at least a day, covering a minimal additional distance (one or two farsakhs) solidifies the ruling, emphasizing intention over continuous movement.
